Cloning, plasmid and lentivirus generation

Through Emory’s Integrated Genomics Core Custom Cloning Division, the TurboID-NES construct (Addgene plasmid #107169) used in our prior study37, was edited to generate a construct without the NES (TurboID-noNES). Restriction enzyme sites were introduced with respective forward and reverse primers (Supplementary Data 1). PCR products were then subcloned into the TurboID-NES backbone. TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES plasmids were transformed into DH5-⍺ competent E. coli cells (NEB, C2987I) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Plasmid DNA was purified following the Miracle-prep (Miraprep) instructions143 (QIAprep Spin Miniprep Kit) and resulting concentration measured using a Qubit. Lentivirus (LV) using the TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES plasmids were generated through Emory’s Viral Vector Core.

In vitro studies

Mouse microglia BV2 cells were cultured in 0.2 µm vacuum filter sterilized Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with high glucose and L-glutamine containing 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 10% fetal bovine serum. BV2 cells were incubated in 100 mm cell culture dish at 37°C and 5% CO until reaching 80-90% confluency. Cells were treated with 100 ng/mL of LPS for 48 h and 200 µM of biotin for 24 h during the second day of LPS treatment.

Human embryonic kidney 293 cells (HEK293) were cultured in DMEM containing 1% penicillin-streptomycin and 10% fetal bovine serum. HEK293 cells were incubated in 6-well culture dishes in the same condition as the BV2 cells described above. At 30% confluency, HEK293 cells were infected with 3 µL of the two LVs generated (TurboID-NES, viral titer: 3.9x108 IU/mL or TurboID-noNES, viral titer: 1.7x109 IU/mL). LV-containing media was removed after 3 days, and successful infection was determined by cellular GFP signal using the ECHO Revolve fluorescence microscope (Echo, USA) prior to lysis. HEK293 cells were grown to 80-90% confluency cells before biotin treatment (200 µM for 24 h).

The 48 h LPS and 24 h biotin treatment paradigms were used to model similar treatment and labeling kinetics for in vivo SPARO studies.

Immunocytochemistry

BV2 control and BV2-TurboID cells were seeded at a density of 1 x 105 cells onto autoclaved and ethanol-treated coverslips placed in a 12-well plate. Seeded cells were treated with 100 ng/mL LPS. After 24 hours, the cells were supplemented with external biotin (200 μM), along with LPS, for an additional 24 hours. After treatments, cells were washed three times with PBS and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Thermo Scientific, J19943-K2) in PBS for 30 min at RT. Fixed cells were permeabilized and blocked simultaneously using 5% goat serum diluted in 0.25% TBST for 1 h at room temperature. Each well was then incubated with 1 mL of antibody cocktail containing rabbit anti-V5 (1:500, Abcam, 206566) and Streptavidin-DyLight 488 (1:500, Invitrogen, 21832) prepared in 1% Goat serum diluted in TBS, overnight at 4 °C. The next day, cells were washed three times with 0.25% TBST, followed by incubation with anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 secondary antibody (1:500, Invitrogen, A21207) prepared in 1% goat serum in TBS for 2 hours at room temperature. Nuclei were stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) for 5 min. After final washes, coverslips were mounted onto glass slides using Fluoromount-G (Invitrogen, 00-4958-02). Images were captured at 60X using a Keyence BZ-X810 microscope.

In vivo studies

Mice were housed in the Division of Animal Resources vivarium at Emory University under a standard environment (12 h light/ 12 h dark cycle, temperature 72°F, humidity range 40-50%) with access to food and water ad libitum. All animal-related studies (PROTO-201700821) were conducted with the approval of Emory’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee following the National Institute of Health’s “Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals” and reported in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines.

Transgenic approach for Cre recombinase expression in neurons and astrocytes using Rosa26TurboID/wt mice:

Neuronal TurboID cohort: Rosa26TurboID/wt (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 037890) were crossed with Camk2aCreERT2 (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 012362) mice to obtain heterozygous Rosa26TurboID/wt/Camk2aCreERT2/wt (“neuron-TurboID”, n = 3, 1 M and 2 F littermate mice. Heterozygous littermate mice Camk2aCreERT2/wt (“Camk2a”, n = 2, 1 M and 1 F) were used as controls.

Astrocytic TurboID cohort: Rosa26TurboID/wt (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 037890) were crossed with Aldh1l1CreERT2 (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 031008) mice to obtain heterozygous Rosa26TurboID/wt/Aldh1l1CreERT2/wt (“astrocyte-TurboID”, n = 8, 6 M and 2 F). Heterozygous littermate mice Aldh1l1CreERT2/wt (“Aldh1l1”, n= 3, 2 M and 1 F) were used as controls. For astrocyte-TurboID LPS studies, systemic LPS at 0.75/kg/dose x 5 days was given via i.p. injection during the first week of biotin water supplementation. Based on previous work and our own, we validated neuron- and astrocyte-specificity and nonleaky Cre activity of the Camk2aCreERT2 and Aldh1l1CreERT2 models, respectively42,59.

Astrocytic RiboTag cohort: RiboTag mice, Rpl22tm1.1Psam (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 029977) were crossed with Aldh1l1CreERT2 (Jackson Labs, Strain No. 031008) mice to obtain heterozygous Rpl22tm1.1Psam/Aldh1l1CreERT2/wt (“astrocyte-RiboTag”, n = 3, 3 F). Heterozygous littermate mice Rpl22tm1.1Psam (“RiboTag”, n= 2, 1 M and 1 F) were used as controls.

All mice were given tamoxifen (75 mg/kg) intraperitoneally (i.p.) for 5 days at 6 weeks of age and allowed 3 weeks of Cre recombination. After Cre recombination, TurboID mice were given water supplemented with biotin (37.5 mg/L) for 2 weeks until euthanasia at 3-4 months of age. RiboTag mice were euthanized at 2.5 months of age. Mice from each cohort were anesthetized using ketamine/xylazine (ketamine 87.5 mg/kg, xylazine 12.5 mg/kg) followed by transcardial perfusion with ice-cold 1X PBS. The brain was immediately removed and hemisected along the mid-sagittal line. The left hemisphere was immediately dissected to obtain the cortex and then snap frozen using dry ice. The right hemisphere was used for immunohistological studies.

Immunohistochemistry

For immunohistochemistry studies, mice were euthanized and perfused with ice-cold 1X PBS, and the brain was dissected. One hemisphere was immediately transferred into 4% PFA (Cat No. J19943.K2) and fixed overnight for immunohistological analysis. After PFA fixation, the brain was washed with 1X PBS 3 times to remove residual PFA and transferred into 30% sucrose solution until sectioning. After removing extra sucrose, the fixed and sucrose-saturated hemisphere was embedded in the Tissue-Tek optimal cutting temperature compound (Cat No. 4583, Sakura) and frozen on dry ice. Serial 40 µm sagittal sections of the brain were generated using a cryostat (Leica Biosystems, CM1850) and stored free-floating in cryoprotective media (Glycerin, Ethylene Glycol and 0.1 M Phosphate Buffer in ratio of 2.5: 3.0: 5.0) at -20°C. For immunofluorescence (IF) staining, 3-4 brain sections from each mouse were washed 3 times with 1X TBS and then blocked and permeabilized by incubating in 1X TBS containing 0.25% Triton X-100 (TBS-T) and 5% goat serum for 1 h at room temperature. Following, sections were incubated with primary antibodies diluted in 1X TBS-T containing 1% goat serum overnight at 4°C. Next, the sections were washed 3X with 1X TBS and then incubated with fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature in the dark. All primary and secondary antibodies were used at dilution 1:500 including HA-tag (Cell Signaling Technology, 3724S), S100β (Proteintech, 15146-1-AP), βIII-Tubulin (Biolegend, 802001), Streptavidin Protein, DyLight™ 488, and Donkey anti-Rabbit- Alexa Fluor™ 594. Brain sections were then incubated for 5 minutes in nuclear staining reagent DAPI (1 µg/mL) dissolved in 1X TBS. The samples were further washed 3X with 1X TBS, mounted onto glass slides and coverslipped using ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (P36965, ThermoFisher). Images of the same brain regions for each mouse were captured using a Keyence fluorescence microscope (Keyence BZ-X810). Images were processed and analyzed using Image J software (FIJI Version 2.14).

Cell and tissue homogenization

BV2 control, BV2-TurboID, HEK293 control, HEK293-TurboID-NES and HEK293-TurboID-noNES cells were washed three times with cold 1X PBS containing 100 µg/mL of cycloheximide. Next, cells were incubated with 1 mL of cold homogenization buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 supplemented with 0.5 mM DTT, 0.1% v/v RNasin, 0.1% v/v SUPERasin, 1X HaltTM protease and phosphatase inhibitors, 100 µg/mL cycloheximide) for 10 minutes, scaped and collected into a 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube. For brain samples, frozen Camk2a and Aldh1l1 controls and neuron-TurboID and astrocyte-TurboID mouse cortices (up to 50 mg) were lysed in same cold homogenization buffer as the BV2 cells with RNase-free glass beads and a Bullet Blender Homogenizer (Next Advance). RiboTag control and astrocyte-RiboTag mouse cortices were lysed in cold RiboTag homogenization buffer (50 mH Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl, 12 mM MgCl2, 1% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, 1% v/v sodium deoxycholate 0.1% v/v RNasin, 0.1% v/v SUPERasin, 1X Halt protease and phosphatase inhibitors, 100 µg/mL cycloheximide) similarly to the TurboID samples. All homogenates underwent 3 rounds of sonication (5 s of active sonication at 25% amplitude followed by a 10 s incubation on ice) followed by centrifugation for 10 min at 2000 x g at 4°C. The supernatants were transferred to a new tube and protein concentrations were calculated using a Pierce BCA assay for proteomic studies. To account for variability in infection efficiency, the HEK293 cell lysates per condition (control uninfected, TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES) were pooled prior to streptavidin affinity purification.

Immunoblotting

To confirm the presence of biotinylated proteins, 17 µg of cell or tissue lysates were resolved on a 4-12% Bis-Tris gel, transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane, blocked with StartingBlock for 30 min and then probed with a streptavidin-AlexaFluor 680 antibody (ThermoFisher, S32358, dilution: 1:10,000 in StartingBlock) for 1 h at room temperature. To confirm TurboID construct presence, the membrane was probed with a rabbit anti-V5 primary antibody (dilution: 1:500 in StartingBlock) overnight and then incubated with a goat anti-rabbit HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111-035-003, dilution: 1:10,000 in StartingBlock). Immunoblots were imaged with an Odyssey Infrared Imaging System (LI-COR Biosciences), or BioRad chemiluminescence system.

Biotinylated protein and ribosomal protein enrichment for transcriptomics

Following confirmation of biotinylated proteins and V5 presence via immunoblotting, biotin-tagged proteins were enriched for using streptavidin-coated magnetic beads36. For each sample in the BV2, astrocyte-TurboID and neuron-TurboID studies, 25 µL of streptavidin beads (ThermoFisher, 88817) in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube were washed 3 times with 1 mL of homogenization buffer on rotation for 2 min. The streptavidin beads were incubated with 300 µg of protein lysate from each sample with additional wash buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 supplemented with 0.5 mM DTT, 1% v/v NP-40 substitute, 0.1 % v/v RNasin, 0.1% v/v SUPERasin, 1X HaltTM protease and phosphatase inhibitors, 100 µg/mL cycloheximide) to create a final volume of 250 µL on rotation for 1 h at 4°C. For the HEK293 studies, 17 µL of streptavidin beads and 200 µg of protein lysate from each pooled sample was used. Next, the beads were washed four times with cold high salt buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 350 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 supplemented with 0.5 mM DTT, 1% v/v NP-40 substitute, 0.1 % v/v RNasin, 0.1% v/v SUPERasin, 1X HaltTM protease and phosphatase inhibitors). After RiboTag control and Astrocyte-RiboTag cortical lysis, 800 µL of lysate was incubated with 4 µL of anti-hemagglutinin (HA) antibody (Biolegend, 901513) for 4 hours on end-over-end rotation at 4°C. For each sample, 25 µL of A/G beads (ThermoFisher, 88803) in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube were washed 3 times with 400 µL of RiboTag homogenization buffer. The A/G beads were incubated with 100 µL of HA-tagged lysate overnight on end-over-end rotation at 4°C. Next, the A/G beads were washed four times with cold RiboTag high salt buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH: 7.5, 300 mM KCl, 12 mM MgCl2, 1% v/v NP-40, 0.50 mM DTT, 100 µg/mL cycloheximide).10 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 350 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 supplemented with 0.5 mM DTT, 1% v/v NP-40 substitute, 0.1 % v/v RNasin, 0.1% v/v SUPERasin, 1X HaltTM protease and phosphatase inhibitors). After final washes, the streptavidin and A/G beads were resuspended in 100 µL of wash buffer and then added to 700 µL of Trizol and stored at -80°C until RNA extraction. For global/input lysate/animal, 50 µL of lysate remained at 4°C during the protein enrichment protocols.

RNA extraction

After protein enrichment using streptavidin and A/B beads, RNA was extracted from the beads and or global lysates using a miRNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen Inc., 217004) following the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA was eluted in RNase-free water and analyzed for purity and concentration using either an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer with the RNA 6000 Nano or Pico Kit, or Agilent 4200 TapeStation System prior to RNA-sequencing library preparation.

RNA-sequencing and processing

After assessing RNA quality, cDNA library preparation was performed. The SMART-Seq® v4 PLUS Kit (Takara Bio) was used following the manufacturer’s protocol. For small RNA-sequencing library preparation, a QIAseq miRNA NGS kit (Qiagen, 331565) was used. Global sequencing of 40 million paired-end reads per sample was completed using the Illumina-based platform at Admera Health. FASTQ files were evaluated for quality using FastQC144 and then mapped to the mouse genome, GRCm38 (mm10), or GRCh38, human genome (hg38), using the Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR)145 (for mRNA-seq) or Bowtie 2146 (for smRNA-seq) aligners with the paired-end option. The featureCounts147 package was used to generate a raw counts data matrix from mapped reads. Lowly abundant transcripts across all samples (average count value ≤ 10) were filtered out. After generating the filtered, raw counts data matrices, we used DESeq2148 to normalize the matrices and perform differential gene expression-based statistics. For astrocyte-TurboID versus astrocyte-RiboTag studies, we used the same astrocyte samples used in neuron-TurboID comparison. RNA-sequencing was completed independently and the resulting FASTQ files were processed and analyzed together. For the Zhang et al., 201460 transcriptomes versus the Sharma et al., 201562 proteomes of acutely isolated astrocytes and neurons, lowly abundant transcripts were filtered out using an average FPKM value of ≤ 3.

Biotinylated or HA-tagged polyribosome protein enrichment for proteomics

For each sample in the BV2, astrocyte-TurboID and neuron-TurboID studies, 42 µL of streptavidin beads in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube were washed 2 times with 1 mL of RIPA lysis buffer (50 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% SDS, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 1% Triton X-100) on rotation for 2 min. The beads were incubated with 500 µg of protein lysate from each sample with additional RIPA lysis buffer to create a final volume of 500 µL on rotation for 1 h at 4°C. For the HEK293 studies, 13 µL of streptavidin beads and 150 µg of protein lysate from each pooled sample was used. Next, the beads were quickly centrifuged, placed on a magnetic rack and the supernatant was transferred to a new 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube and stored at -80°C. The beads were washed with the following buffers on rotation at room temperature: twice with 1 mL of RIPA lysis buffer for 8 min, once with 1 M KCl for 8 min, once with 1 mL 0.1 M sodium carbonate for ~10 s, once with 1 mL 2 M urea in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6) for ~10 s, and twice with 1 mL RIPA lysis buffer for 8 min. After the final RIPA wash, the beads were resuspended in 1 mL of 1X PBS, transferred to a new tube and washed two more times with 1X PBS on rotation for 2 min. To confirm biotinylated protein enrichment, 10% of the streptavidin bead volume was transferred to a new 1.5 mL Eppendorf LoBind tube and boiled in 30 μL of 2X Laemmli protein loading buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610737) supplemented with 2 mM biotin and 20 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 95°C for 10 min to elute the biotinylated proteins. Following, 1/3 or the eluate was resolved on a 4-12% Bis-Tris gel, transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane, blocked with StartingBlock for 30 min and incubated overnight with a rabbit anti-V5 antibody (Abcam, ab206566) on a shaker at 4°C. Next, the membrane was incubated with a goat anti-rabbit HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111-035-003, dilution: 1:10,000 in StartingBlock) and streptavidin-AlexaFluor 680 antibody (ThermoFisher, S32358, dilution: 1:10,000 in StartingBlock) for 1 h at room temperature. The remaining 2/3 of protein eluate was resolved on a 4-12% Bis-Tris gel for a silver stain (ThermoFisher, 24612). Immunoblots were imaged with an Odyssey Infrared Imaging System (LI-COR Biosciences), or BioRad chemiluminescence system. Silver-stained gels were imaged using a Canon scanner (CanoScan LIDE 300).

For astrocyte-RiboTag-based proteomics of HA-tagged polyribosomes and associated proteins, 50 µL of A/G beads were incubated with 200 µL of anti-HA lysate per sample. This ratio was used to approximately match the astrocyte-TurboID bead to lysate ratio. The rest of the protocol matched the RNA pulldowns with the addition of RNA depletion via 50 µg/mL of RNaseA (Thermo Scientific, EN0531) in PBS for 15 min at room temperature on end-to-end rotation. After, the beads were washed 3 times with PBS prior to preparation for MS.

Protein digestion

To prepare enriched biotinylated proteins from BV2, astrocyte-TurboID, and neuron-TurboID for MS-based proteomics, the remaining 90% volume of the streptavidin beads were resuspended in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (Na2CO3). Next, the bound proteins were reduced with 1 mM DTT for 30 min at room temperature and then alkylated with 5 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) in the dark for 30 min. Following, proteins were subsequently digested overnight with 0.5 µg of lysyl (Lys-C) endopeptidase (Wako, 127-06621) and then 1 µg of trypsin (ThermoFisher, 90058) on the shaker at room temperature. After digestion, the resulting peptide mixtures were acidified to a final concentration of 1% formic acid and 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid, desalted with an HLB column (Waters, 186003908), and dehydrated using a vacuum centrifuge (SpeedVac Vacuum Concentrator). The same approach was used for HA-tagged polyribosomes from astrocyte-RiboTag samples. To prepare global lysates for MS-proteomics, 50 µg of protein from each sample was reduced in 5 mM DTT for 30 min at room temperature and then alkylated with 10 mM IAA for 30 min in the dark. After, each sample was diluted (4-fold) with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC) buffer and then digested with 1 µg of Lys-C endopeptidase on the shaker overnight at room temperature. Next, samples were diluted (4-fold) with 50 mM ABC buffer and digested with 2 µg of trypsin on the shaker overnight at room temperature. After digestion, the peptide mixtures were acidified, desalted, and dried down as described above.

To prepare enriched biotinylated proteins from HEK293 TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES samples for MS-based proteomics, the remaining 90% of the streptavidin beads were resuspended in 5% SDS in 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB). Proteins were reduced with 10 mM DTT for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by alkylation with 20 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) in the dark for 30 minutes. The proteins were then acidified with phosphoric acid. A mixture of 100 mM TEAB and 90% methanol (MeOH) was added, and the samples were transferred to S-Trap micro spin columns (Protifi). Binding and washing steps were performed according to the S-Trap protocol. Digestion was carried out by adding 0.5 µg Lys-C and 1 µg trypsin, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 18 hours. Peptides were eluted sequentially with 50 mM TEAB, 0.2% formic acid, and 50% acetonitrile, then dried using a SpeedVac. The same protocol was followed for the global lysates with 25 µg of protein from each sample used as input. Peptide concentration was determined by fluorescence-based BCA assay. Finally, samples were injected volumetrically into the mass spectrometer.

Mass spectrometry

Mass spectrometry preparation and acquisition parameters were selected based on conditions established in our prior work31,33,36 and detailed here. For BV2, astrocyte-TurboID, and neuron-TurboID studies, dried peptides were reconstituted in 15 µL of loading solution (0.1% formic acid and 0.03% trifluoroacetic acid in water), and 7-8 µL was injected onto a self-packed 25 cm analytical column (100 µm inner diameter) packed with 1.7 µm Waters CSH particles. Peptides were separated using either an Easy-nLC 1200 or a Dionex 3000 RSLCnano nanoLC system. The gradient began at 1% solvent B (80% acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid) and increased to 5% over 10 seconds, followed by a 55-minute linear gradient to 35% solvent B. The run concluded with a 4-minute, 50-second wash at 99% solvent B. Following, an Orbitrap Lumos Tribrid MS with a high-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS Pro)149 interface was used to obtain all mass spectra at a compensation voltage of -45V. BV2-TurboID in vitro and astrocyte-TurboID and neuron-TurboID in vivo studies were completed using data-dependent acquisition (DDA) LFQ-MS using top-speed mode with a 3 s cycle time. Full MS scans were acquired in the Orbitrap at 120,000 resolution across an m/z range of 400-1,600, with an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 400,000, a maximum injection time of 50 ms, and the RF lens set to 30%. MS/MS spectra were generated by higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) and analyzed in the ion trap using a normalized collision energy of 35% and an isolation window of 0.7 m/z. The AGC target for MS/MS scans was 10,000 with a maximum injection time of 35 ms. Dynamic exclusion was enabled for 30 s with a mass tolerance window of 10 ppm.

For astrocyte-RiboTag and HEK293 studies, dried peptides were separated on a 75 µm x 60 cm analytical column (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using a 135-min (astrocyte-RiboTag) or 115-min (HEK293) gradient from 1-99% solvent B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) at 300 nL/min. MS analysis was performed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in positive ion mode. Full MS scans were acquired at 120,000 resolution (m/z 400-1000), and data-independent-acquisition (DIA) MS/MS scans at 30,000 resolution (m/z 150-2000) using 10 m/z isolation windows with 1 m/z overlap and HCD fragmentation at 28% normalized collision energy.

Protein identification and quantification

DDA raw MS files for global and pulldown protein from BV2-TurboID in vitro and astrocyte- and neuron-TurboID in vivo studies along with respective controls were searched separately using the Andromeda150 search engine integrated into MaxQuant151 (version v2.4.2.0), against the 2020 downloaded mouse UniProt proteome (https://www.uniprot.org/proteomes/UP000000589) including sequences for V5 and TurboID. DIA Raw MS files from the astrocyte-RiboTag pulldown and the HEK293-TurboID (NES versus noNES) global and pulldown experiments were searched separately using the Pulsar search engine integrated into Spectronaut (version 19)152. The astrocyte-RiboTag search was performed against the same 2020 mouse UniProt proteome described above (with the HA sequence included). The HEK293-TurboID studies were searched against the 2025 downloaded human UniProt proteome (https://www.uniprot.org/proteomes/UP000005640). Search parameters were determined by our prior work31,33,36,37,153 and described here. Methionine oxidation (+15.9949 Da) and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.0106 Da) were variable modifications (up to 5 allowed per peptide); cysteine was assigned as a fixed carbamidomethyl modification (+57.0215 Da). Only fully tryptic peptides were considered with up to 2 missed cleavages in the database search. A precursor mass tolerance of +/-20 ppm was applied prior to mass accuracy calibration and +/-4.5 ppm after internal calibration. Other search settings included a maximum peptide mass of 4600 Da, a minimum peptide length of 6 residues, 0.05 Da tolerance for Orbitrap and 0.6 Da tolerance for ion trap MS/MS scans. Quantification settings were as follows: re-quantify with a second peak finding attempt after protein identification has completed; match MS1 peaks between runs; a 0.7 min retention time match window was used after an alignment function was found with a 20 min RT search space. Peptide spectral match false discovery rate (FDR) was set to 1%. The MaxQuant or Spectronaut output data (raw intensity values) were uploaded to R (version 4.3.1) for normalization, log transformation, and differential abundance analyses.

To account for endogenously biotinylated and non-specific proteins captured during streptavidin affinity purification, mean intensity values from TurboID-negative control pulldown samples were subtracted from the TurboID-positive pulldown samples by group. To account for variability in TurboID expression, biotinylated protein abundance, and streptavidin affinity purification efficiency, intensity values were normalized depending on the dataset. For BV2 in vitro studies comparing the abundance values from global protein and enriched pulldown samples, samples were normalized by taking each sample’s log-transformed summed protein intensity median and setting it to zero. The BV2-TurboID pulldown groups (untreated and LPS-treated) intensity values were normalized based on TurboID abundance. We did not find a difference in TurboID abundance in the other SPARO datasets, so this normalization approach was only completed on the BV2-TurboID pulldown groups. For astrocyte-TurboID and neuron-TurboID in vivo studies, enriched pulldown samples were normalized by subtracting the difference from the mean of the log-transformed summed protein intensity for 71 ribosomal subunit proteins present in all TurboID-positive pulldown samples. Proteins were filtered out if they had missing values in 2/3 samples across groups. Missing values were imputed from normal distribution for each sample. Nomination of proteins as either ribosomal or RNA-binding were determined using the EMBL RBPbase (v0.23 alpha), a database that integrates high-throughput RNA-binding protein detection studies (https://apps.embl.de/rbpbase/).

Data analysis and visualization

We utilized differential enrichment analysis, multidimensional scaling (MDS), and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) to analyze transcriptomic and proteomic data from in vitro and in vivo studies. Data analysis and visualization was completed using R software (version 4.3.1) and Prism (GraphPad, version 10). Venn diagrams were generated using either a protein missingness (present in 2/3 samples) or low abundant transcript (average count value ≤ 10) filter per sample group. For transcriptomic studies, the DESeq2148 Wald test was used to identify DEGs between groups. For proteomic studies, unpaired two-sided (equal variance assumption) t test equivalent calculations using F value from ANOVA run strictly with 2 comparison groups were performed with the parANOVA suite of functions in R (https://github.com/edammer/parANOVA) to identify DEPs between groups. DEGs and DEPs are presented as volcano plots. GSEA was applied using the GOparallel function (https://github.com/edammer/GOparallel) that scrapes monthly updated .GMT formatted GO from the Bader Lab website (https://baderlab.org/) as gene symbol lists submitted to one-tailed Fisher’s exact test for GO enrichment of overlapping symbols in gene lists of interest, including DEPs and DEGs. GO terms meeting Fisher exact significance of p value ≤ 0.05 (i.e., a z ≥ 1.96) were considered. Protein and gene input lists were significantly differentially biochemically enriched over global or background, in addition to gene lists that were different by treatment condition (p ≤ 0.05, ≥ 1-log -fold change). To assess average GC content, number of exons, and average transcript length of transcriptomic data, we used the biomaRt R package154,155 and the BioMart/Ensembl databases156. To examine protein half-life information of proteomic data, we used values from Fornasiero et al., 201868.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
- What are the noteworthy results?
In this paper, the authors claim to have developed a new approach that allows simultaneous cell type specific RNA and
proteomic profiling by adapting TurboID. Specific claims include:
1) TURBO ID allows enrichment-via-biotinlyation of both cytosolic RNA and protein.
2) This was validated in an in vitro system (BV2) cells
3) The method is sensitive enough to detect changes in response to a stimulus known to change proteome and
transcriptome (LPS on BV2 cells).
4) The method works in vivo as tested in comparing neurons to astrocytes (comparing to existing benchmark data)
5) They examine mRNA/protein concordance & discordance and report how this pattern differs by cell at the level of GO
terms.
They also generally argue this will be a useful method for biological discoveries in the future.
- Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields?
Being able to simultaneously measure RNA and protein in the same cell type, in vivo, is a potentially transformative
advance. As such, this is a very clever adaptation of existing tools, and a neat proof of concept study comparing two cell
types in the brain. I think it could open up new questions on gene and protein regulation in the brain and represents a nice
body of work potentially suitable for this journal. But, it is a bit fuzzy on what kind of new questions one could ask with it right
now. I have a couple of recommendations below of where they could address that. On the whole, I think it is a quite cool
idea, but it could benefit from a more concrete description of a couple clear use cases.
How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references.
It reminds me a bit of Alice Ting’s Apex-Seq, but since that requires Biotin-Phenol I am not sure it would work in vivo, but it
might be worth comparing this to that a bit in discussion or intro.
- Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
For the most part, the work does support the conclusions. But it is a bit unclear where the authors think this new approach
might make impact in the future. For example, this is a rather vague sentence to lead off the discussion: “Measuring
transcriptomic and proteomic levels is important to identify cellular and molecular mechanisms of biology.” The last para of
the discussion also has several similarly vague sentences about the contribution this new method could make. Can the
authors make these sections more concrete?
In general the discussion is a bit of a missed opportunity, as it spends a larger balance of the space restating the findings
and less time on describing that would be done next. Or discussing technical considerations on implementing this. For
example, is this time course of labeling required (something that might be addressed in experiments, see below)?
There is also probably one more set of experiments needed to understand the noise of the method in general (see ‘Is the
Methodology Sound’ section).
- Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
Overall, I view my comments as requiring revision rather than prohibiting publication.
Figure S7d: TurboID and RiboTag have substantial differences (thousands of DEGs in Figure S10) that are rather
underplayed here. I would recommend a couple of analyses digging into these differences more. Maybe something similar to
what they do in Figure S10?
The authors spend some time on page 8 speculating why the transcriptome and proteome are sometimes discordant. One
additional source of such discordance could simply be cellular compartment: it seems like even in vivo the TURBO-ID is
restricted to the cytoplasm? Yet the transcripts that code for all proteins in the cell (nuclear, mitochondria, etc), are largely
translated in the cytoplasm. So some of the discordance could simply reflect that the mature translated protein ends up
somewhere in the cell where it cannot be readily tagged. Likewise, any excreted proteins might be lost to TurboID labeling
(including potentially Lcn2, which they highlight in their discussion). When the come back discussing discordance on page
10, they do bring up this possibility that it is driven by cellular compartments in part. However, they may wish to revise these
sections, as the different cellular compartments is probably the simplest explanation and should be raised earlier.
The difficulty in interpreting RNA/Protein comparisons is the part of the paper I find the most challenging and that would
make me hesitant to bring the approach into my own lab. Is there anything that could be done informatically to address this?
For example, if they limit the analysis comparing RNA to Protein to the proteins that are in the cytoplasm (potentially by GO),
does the correlation improve between RNA and Protein? Does the ability to use things like protein half lives (or perhaps
codon usage) to predict Protein/RNA discordance improve? And can they start to look at cell differences in RNA/Protein
discordance in a more insightful way if limiting their analysis to proteins that have a better chance of being tagged (i.e., the
cytoplasmic ones)? On the whole, this comparisons seems to be one of the motivating aspects of the paper, so it would be
nice to have some recommendations on how to approach these questions with the current technique. (I appreciate that the
authors also discuss future method changes like removing the NES that might address this experimentally).
- Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
They need to better account for sex in their work (and in future studies, may want to balance for it, though there is clearly no
way to travel back in time to change samples now). For example, in Figure 2i. Did the neuron line samples have more
females than the astrocyte line samples? Otherwise can the authors explain why Xist (a female-only transcript) is a top
gene? Actually, this comes up across several other figures (e.g., Fig S7d, which also shows a lot of Y chromosome genes).
Ah, as I get to discussion, it does seem like the sexes were not well balanced in the experiment. Hmm.. the authors may
wish to flag sex-chromosome derived ‘DEG/DEPs’ as being potential false positives (driven by sex rather than cell type)
with a column in their supplemental tables and explicitly exclude them from volcano plots.
The method would benefit from a more quantitative characterization of the noise, as it is a new method. Did the author
sequence mouse brain samples that did not have the Turbo allele? I agree from the tapestations there is less RNA coming
down without it, but some is still there. Knowing what is in that RNA (and potentially filtering/subtracting it from the true
samples) is important to characterize noise, eliminate sources of false positives in some analyses (e.g., Riboseq vs. their
method) and potentially improve signal to noise in the future. Potentially similar experiments might be done with proteomics
too.
Can the authors address to what extent is it necessary to feed the animals biotin? I assume there is some biotin present in
the cells in vivo regardless. How does signal change with vs. without the added biotin in the diet?
Likewise, is there a relatively cheap and fast way to explore how features of the biotin pulse to the animal change the yield
(like just I.F. or quantifying tape station, streptavidin immunoblot or silver stain) that would give a sense of how much the
timing and magnitude of that pulse needs to be optimized by labs adopting this approach? Or if this is already done in prior
papers, perhaps allude to that in methods.
- Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced?
Yes. The methods were clearly written.
Typos/minor notes:
Should the A be underlined and bolded when defining the acronym for SPARO?
Figure 1l disagrees with the results text on the magnitude of a correlation (.68 vs .83).
Figure 1 legend about 1d: mRNA is usually not visible on a tapestation, just the rRNA.
“Hepacam, Glu, Aqp4, Plpp3, p ≤ 0.05, ≥ 1-fold change” should this be “> 1 log2 fold-change”?
Figure S10: If you calculate a logFC of RNA vs Protein, can you then compare the protein half lives to that? For ‘a’ does
seem to be a relationship between quadrant and protein half life coloration, though it seems to disappear by b and c. Being
able to more directly compare Protein/RNA to half life might have more explanatory power.
I am also confused by the next sentence “Less than 5% of gene products exhibit cell type-specific expression patterns (via >
4-fold enrichment), and as a result, bulk tissue -omics studies cannot completely resolve changes occurring at the level of
individual cell types55,59” I am trying to understand how the first clause of the sentence results in the second clause.
“which is in line with prior studies57–59” can the authors highlight more quantitatively the extent of correlation seen in prior
studies? Is it similar to their .24-27 (Figure S8) Are their bulk results (.47) more comparable in magnitude of correlation to
those prior studies?
This sentence does not make much sense “There are also limited resources to determine which allele of a gene yields a
particular protein isoform.” Aren’t all these mice inbred? And thus homozygous at most alleles?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
NCOMMS-25-08576
Simultaneous profiling of native-state proteomes and transcriptomes of neural cell types using proximity labeling
The manuscript by Ramelow et al. outlines the development and application of a novel method for complementary profiling
of cell type-specific proteomes and transcriptomes called “SPARO” (simultaneous protein and RNA -omics). They validate
their approach using a microglial cell line in vitro and then in neurons and astrocytes in vivo using the same mouse lines for
cell type-specific, cytosolic expression of biotin ligase TurboID that they described previously in Rayaprolu et al., 2022,
Nature Communications. The main difference between the work in this manuscript and their previous work is that they
perform both proteomics and transcriptomics to investigate the correlation between mRNA and protein abundances, of which
is a useful analysis to glean insight on post-transcriptional regulatory processes. Owing to the cell type-specificity of their
approach, the authors compare the concordance between neuronal and astrocytic proteomes and transcriptomes. Although
SPARO, in theory, builds upon their previously published work, there are limitations that need to be addressed in order for
them to complete a meaningful assessment of mRNA/protein concordance. As is, the conclusions made from their
mRNA/protein concordance analysis are lackluster and lack experimental validation.
Major criticisms/suggestions:
1. Regarding Fig.1: The drastic difference in TurboID expression between LPS-treated and non-treated BV2 cells is
concerning. Why is the expression in the non-treated cells (as indicated by the V5 immunolabeling in Fig.1c) about half of
that in the LPS-treated cells? The streptavidin labeling is also dramatically different between the LPS-treated and untreated
cells (Fig.1c/Fig.S1a). To be able to compare the LPS-treated and nontreated transcriptomes/proteomes, the level of
cytosolic TurboID expression needs to be similar. Otherwise, differences in mRNA and protein abundances may reflect
differences in the extent of biotinylation/labeling, rather than bona fide differences in expression. In the methods, the authors
outline how they perform median centering of the log2 transformed intensity values to account for variability in TurboID
expression, biotinylated protein abundance, and streptavidin affinity purification efficiency. Given the magnitude of these
differences however, I am not confident that this normalization method is sufficient. For their transcriptomic data analysis, the
authors do not account for this variability. In Fig.1e, the LPS pulldown proteome has almost 20% more proteins than the non-
LPS pulldown proteome. In Fig.1f, the LPS pulldown transcriptome has 58% more mRNAs. Is this reflecting true changes in
protein/mRNA abundances or is it because of differences in the extent of biotinylation/labeling?
2. Regarding Fig.1: Does the 48 h LPS treatment lead to increased expression of TurboID? This needs to be investigated
and taken into consideration when interpreting results. The authors should include immunofluorescent images and
quantification of the V5 and streptavidin labeling of the BV2 control cells and BV2-TurboID cells before and after LPS (or
mock) treatment.
3. Throughout the manuscript, the authors mistakenly attribute what is likely Agilent TapeStation images as “RNA gel
electrophoresis”. The authors need to relabel this (perhaps as “RNA ScreenTape analysis” or something similar) because
the Agilent TapeStation does not use traditional gel electrophoresis, but rather microfluidics. The details are missing in the
methods. The authors state that “high levels of rRNA and mRNA were detected”, but there are no real bands except the 28S
RNA (~4000 nt) and 18S rRNA (~2000 nt) bands in Fig.1d. The authors should perform standard RNA polyacrylamide gel
electrophoresis instead.
4. Overall, validation of their findings is lacking (e.g., LPS treatment experiments in Fig.1 and Fig.S6). Validation (e.g.,
immunofluorescence imaging) is essential.
5. Regarding Fig.1e: The authors find only ~50% overlap between the biotinylated cytosolic proteome and the bulk
proteomes. They say that this is likely because the biotinylated cytosolic proteome doesn’t contain the proteomes of the
nuclear and mitochondrial compartments. The authors should look into this further to back up their claim. Why not subset
their bulk proteome data for cytosolic proteins and then do the comparison? Biotinylation by TurboID requires certain amino
acids to be present in a given protein and accessible. The authors could also determine the extent of the cytosolic proteome
(using annotated datasets) that is captured in the pulldown proteome and check to see which, if any, cytosolic proteins aren’t
being captured.
6. Regarding Fig.3: The authors compare the abundance/enrichment of ribosomal proteins in the cre-only control vs.
astrocyte-TurboID pulldowns and are able to capture 66 RPs and 67 RNA-binding proteins. A more important comparison
would be between the astrocyte-TurboID pulldown and the astrocyte-RiboTag HA IP eluate.
7. Regarding Fig.3: The authors state that “a notable difference between the SPARO and RiboTag transcriptomes is that in
SPARO, TurboID biotinylates 133 proteins that interact with RNA (e.g., ribosomal and RBPs), while the RiboTag approach
labels one ribosomal protein”. To back up their claim, the authors should report how many of these 133 proteins are detected
in the RiboTag IP HA eluates. I would assume that several RBPs will be detected, even without UV crosslinking.
8. Regarding Fig.4: Without whole-cell TurboID expression, mRNA/protein concordance analysis is problematic. A major
point of simultaneous proteomic/transcriptomic profiling is to be able to do this analysis in the first place. With cytosolic
TurboID, even with 2 weeks of labeling, caution and care needs to be taken in interpreting the mRNA/protein concordance
for luminal proteins localized within membrane-bound organelles as well as any protein localized within
double-membrane-bound organelles. The highly discordant genes (mRNA >> protein) related to mitochondria in both astrocytes
and neurons should be validated. Is the observed discordance because these mRNAs are co-translationally imported at the OMM,
and therefore escaping cytosolic biotinylation?
9. Validation of mRNA-protein discordant astrocytic/neuronal markers is lacking.
Minor criticisms/suggestions:
1. The gain should be increased in the silver stain image in Fig.S1c. The figure legend states that “several proteins were
enriched in the BV2-TurboID samples”, but it’s not obvious.
2. The authors mention how assessments of protein/mRNA concordance are confounded by differences in the sensitivity of
LFQ-MS and RNA-sequencing. Did they authors do data-independent acquisition (DIA), which is more sensitive than data-
dependent acquisition (DDA)?
3. In the discussion, the authors mention potential brain region-specific differences. Why do the authors not compare their
data (cortex) with the Soto et al., 2023 dataset (striatum)?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, Ramelow and co-authors present SPARO, a new method to simultaneously measure transcriptomes and
proteomes from living systems. They first benchmark this method against global transcriptomics and global proteomics using
an in vitro model, then go on to apply this method in an in vivo mouse model to simultaneously capture cell-type specific
proteomes and transcriptomes in the brain. From this data, they go on to interrogate protein-mRNA concordance and
discordance across cell types.
I enjoyed reading this manuscript, and I think that this method would be a valuable addition to the scientific community. The
in vivo cell-type specific profiling in particular was quite compelling, and certainly addresses a technological gap. I do,
however, have some questions and concerns that I would like to see addressed prior to recommending for publication. I
acknowledge that there are many points raised below, but I will preface that I am not asking for any additional experiments - I
would just like some clarification on the authors' methodologies and interpretation of the data, the inclusion of some
additional analyses, and more discussion in the main text on the points outlined below.
My major concerns are largely surrounding the in vitro method validation upon which the rest of the work is based, in
particular the technical robustness of both the transcriptomic and proteomic components of the TurboID enrichment method
for SPARO and the MS data acquisition and analysis. Due to these concerns, I also do not think this method would be
suitable for spatial transcriptomics as mentioned in the discussion. Further, due to the bias introduced by TurboID labeling,
I have concerns for SPARO being used to characterize RNA/protein concordance and discordance, although I do recognize
that it could still be very useful for comparing changes in these patterns between conditions and for proposing proteomic or
transcriptomic biomarkers. Below I have outlined these concerns and others, as well as some minor points to be addressed:
1. I appreciate the time the authors took in the introduction to discuss other technologies in this space to highlight current
gaps, however there were two additional methods that I recommend the authors include. The first is CITE-Seq from Illumina,
which allows simultaneous quantitation of transcriptomes and proteins from single cells - I think the differences (and
advantages) of SPARO are quite easy to highlight (limited panel of proteins that can be quantified in CITE-seq, custom
antibody reliance, cost). The other more relevant methods are APEX-seq and CAP-seq (see publications below), which are
other proximity labeling methods that can be used to capture cell-type specific proteomes and transcriptomes using very
similar workflows to SPARO. The main differences are that first, the proximity labeling enzymes used in these methods,
APEX2 and miniSOG, can biotinylate nucleic acids directly like they can biotinylate proteins, which could allow for fewer
false negatives compared to SPARO (although looking at the high correlation between your SPARO transcriptomes and
global transcriptomes, I don’t think this is actually an issue), but also allows harsh washing through the entire enrichment
protocol which could allow for fewer false positives (which I am concerned could be an issue for SPARO). The second major
difference is that these methods require either the addition of hydrogen peroxide (APEX2) or light (miniSOG) to initiate
labeling, therefore they would most likely need to be done ex-vivo (although there are a few in vivo studies for both).
SPARO has a clear advantage here, as the simple biotin labeling allows for non-invasive, live labeling in the intact animal.
a. Fazal, F. M. et al. (2019) Atlas of Subcellular RNA localization revealed by APEX-seq. Cell, 178, 473-490.
b. Padron, A. et al. (2019) Proximity RNA labeling by APEX-seq reveals the organization of translational initiation
complexes and repressive RNA granules. Molecular Cell, 75, 875-887.
c. Li, R. et al. (2022) Metabolic incorporation of electron-rich ribonucleosides enhances APEX-seq for profiling spatially
restricted nascent transcriptome. Cell Chemical Biology, 29, 1218-1231.
d. Wang, P. et al. (2019) Mapping spatial transcriptome with light-activated proximity-dependent RNA labeling.
Nature Chemical Biology, 15, 1110-1119.
2. Why did you choose to carry out the TurboID biotinylation for 24 hours? This is quite excessive to the 10 min labeling time
recommended for in vitro overexpression systems, particularly for the TurboID-NES construct. Yet, I was surprised to see
that the extent of biotinylation observed in the streptavidin blot of whole cell lysates was much lower than what I would have
expected for this long of a labeling period (Supplementary Figure 1a, comparing the biotinylation signal in the +TurboID
samples to the signal from the endogenously biotinylated proteins). Are your TurboID expression levels very low? Also,
does it appear that TurboID expression and thus biotinylation increases with LPS stimulation? If so, what are your thoughts
about this? It would be nice to have the V5 blot shown for the whole-cell lysate blots in addition to the pulldown blots.
3. I am a bit concerned about the efficiency of your pulldown, as there is robust biotinylation shown in the whole cell lysate
(Fig S1a) but very little in the eluate (Fig. 1c, S1c), in the silver it looks like it’s mostly endogenously biotinylated proteins
pulled down? Did you blot your flow through to show that you successfully depleted your whole cell lysate of biotinylated
material? Inefficient capture could explain the low now numbers you see in your MS data.
4. Does Figure 1d really show that you only enrich RNA with proteomic biotinylation? While you do have stronger
enrichment of the two darkest bands (rRNA?) with TurboID labeling, it appears to my eye that RNA of other sizes are
actually more strongly enriched in the non-Turbo samples - definitely not “negligible”, looks like many RNAs could be non-
specifically binding. Had you happened to run RNA sequencing on the TurboID negative samples? If so, how many
transcripts did you detect/quantify compared to TurboID positive samples and how do these compare to the bulk RNA seq
data?
5. I am quite concerned that you only quantify 1455 proteins in your global proteome. Honestly, this is very low and a red
flag, so please explain. For global proteomics, I would expect at least 7000 but up to 9000+ proteins. Only 1038 proteins is
also very low for a TurboID enriched proteome. For TurboID-NES, I would expect detection of at least 3000 but up to 5000+
proteins. I know that you state in your discussion that more sensitive MS approaches are likely to increase the depth of the
proteome, but the numbers you have here are far below what would be expected from a Lumos Tribrid MS instrument.
6. Is the fidelity of the TurboID vs global RNA-seq datasets suspicious given the large apparent bias in the proteomics
results that are claimed to be due to nuclear exclusion? Are there not several nuclear specific RNAs that you would expect
to miss for the same reason (not a leading question, genuinely asking as a non-expert)? Could this very high overlap
between the TurboID and global datasets further suggest that many of these RNAs being detected are ones that are being
non-specifically enriched and not due to the TurboID labeling?
7. Figure 1g is honestly a bit confusing for me. What is this dimensional scaling based off of, intensity as stated in the
legend, or log2FC as stated in the figure? If Log2FC, what is the Log2FC based off of since all four conditions are plotted
separately? How are you dealing with missing values? The default imputation option in MaxQuant is probably not the best
for this type of data. I’m not very familiar with MDS, but assuming I can read this like a PCA, this figure is saying that the
differences in proteins detected by global proteomics is lower than the differences detected by TurboID proteomics, but
opposite for the RNA data? Is there a technical or biological reason that would explain this? Could this also be due to batch
effects? DDA LFQ is very sensitive to technical variability, you discuss this caveat as well as tell readers of more reliable
quantitation methods like TMT or DIA in the discussion. As for this MDS plot, please explain more or remove entirely - as is,
this is not very meaningful. Honestly, showing the correlation between methods and the volcanoes within the methods
comparing the +/- LPS may be sufficient to show that you are successfully detecting the effect of LPS using the different
methods.
8. I saw in the methods that you are using a reference proteome from 5 years ago (and an old version of MaxQuant), which is
quite dated considering how often these reference proteomes get updated. Is this simply when the experiment was
conducted? If not, please justify why you are using this as the reference proteome. Also, does this reference proteome match
with the appropriate reference genome for the RNA-seq data? If there are discrepancies this could explain some of the
differences observed instead of being due to the biology.
9. For Fig. 1h, please explain where the 1455 shared proteins are coming from, because Fig. 1e indicates that only 1232
proteins are shared between the +LPS global and pulldown proteomes. Also, there should be more discussion on why there
is such low correlation in the protein abundances between the pulldown and global proteome datasets - likely, it is not
simply due to the nuclear exclusion of TurboID, but also how many solvent-exposed and sterically-accessible lysines a
protein has to be biotinylated by TurboID, how reactive these lysines are, how well a protein is able to be pulled down, etc. A
protein may be very abundant in the cytosol and highly detected by global proteomics, but if it isn’t capable of being labeled
by TurboID then it will not appear in the pulldown data.
10. For Fig. 1i, please explain where the 12742 shared transcripts are coming from, because Fig. 1f indicates that only
11947 transcripts are shared between the +LPS global and pulldown transcriptomes. Again here, I worry that the high
correlation between the global and pulldown datasets is suggestive that most of the RNA signal is not due to TurboID
enrichment. As discussed in the point above, due to the chemical nature of TurboID labeling, there is a bias in the proteins
enriched which I would expect to also bias the associated RNAs being pulled down.
11. Was the same cell lysis/sample preparation used for the global transcriptomics and the RNA enrichment for SPARO?

We wish to thank the reviewers for their thorough and very constructive reviews and suggestions.
All reviewers found consensus strengths in the novelty and application of the SPARO approach.
Several highlighted shared weaknesses related to the “noise”/background of SPARO and
expressed concerns with the TurboID-NES enzyme being cytosolic and how this biases the
findings of the correlation between mRNA-protein abundances.
We have now addressed individual concerns to the best of our abilities, updated our manuscript
with new experiments, additional analyses and discussion, all marked in the revised manuscript
as blue text. We strongly believe that the updated manuscript has been improved after integrating
reviewer recommendations and hope that we have satisfactorily addressed Reviewer comments.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
- What are the noteworthy results?
1. For the most part, the work does support the conclusions. But it is a bit unclear where the
authors think this new approach might make impact in the future. For example, this is a rather
vague sentence to lead off the discussion: “Measuring transcriptomic and proteomic levels is
important to identify cellular and molecular mechanisms of biology.” The last para of the
discussion also has several similarly vague sentences about the contribution this new method
could make. Can the authors make these sections more concrete? In general the discussion is a
bit of a missed opportunity, as it spends a larger balance of the space restating the findings and
less time on describing that would be done next.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback. We have made significant changes to the
Discussion section as suggested. We have first emphasized the gaps in the field and how the
SPARO approach, based on our key findings, overcomes these technical challenges. We have
highlighted the major findings in the initial section of the discussion as well. Towards the end of
the discussion, we have extended the discussion on potential applications of SPARO to different
cell types, tissue types, disease models, sub-regions of organs/tissues as well as the capture of
non-coding RNA species with SPARO. To support this new and exciting application, we have also
included new data where we captured astrocyte-specific microRNA signatures that were distinct
from that of bulk cortical tissue. Furthermore, we have discussed how our SPARO transcriptome
compares to the RiboTag transcriptome, now highlighting what is similar and dissimilar, as
requested by the reviewers. Lastly, we have highlighted limitations of our study, and how future
modifications to the SPARO approach could potentially address these.
2. ...or discussing technical considerations on implementing this [approach]. For example, is
this time course of labeling required (something that might be addressed in experiments, see
below)?
Response: This is an important point and led us to perform a new treatment duration experiment
so we could include a robust discussion on the topic (see below).
The initial reason we chose to use longer labeling paradigms in BV2 cells was to match the
prolonged in vivo time course we had previously established. We acknowledge that the efficiency
of TurboID allows rapid labeling within 10 minutes in cells in culture1. However, because we do
not have such temporal control of labeling in vivo (in the brain), the 24-hour of biotinylation
seemed to be a reasonable starting point, so that both in vitro and in vivo systems would have
similar biotinylation durations. We have observed no cell toxicity with 24-hour paradigms in BV2
cells. As previously published2, we also found minimal impact of 24-hour biotinylation on global
cell proteomes, cell viability or cytokine production in response to lipopolysaccharide or cellular
respiration (Seahorse assay). Furthermore, the 24-hour time point allows for detection of immune-
related, signaling. and scaffold proteins that may not be captured in a shorter treatment window3.
Similarly, when labeling Camk2a-expressing neurons or parvalbumin (PV)-expressing
interneurons with TurboID in vivo4–6, we also did not observe electrophysiological alterations in
both neuronal sub-types despite 2 weeks of biotinylation.
To experimentally address the reviewer’s question about the duration of biotin labeling, we
performed a biotin treatment duration experiment in the Camk2a-CreERT2/TurboID (neuron-
TurboID) mice and found that 1 week of biotin water is sufficient to biotinylate neuronal proteins.
Please see streptavidin immunoblot below. Based on this finding, we predict that 1 week of
biotin water supplementation can be adapted for future studies. The data for this finding is now
included in Supplementary Fig. 6g and below.
We did include +biotin and -biotin immunoblot data in our original in vivo TurboID paper4 showing
that whole cell biotinylation levels in HEK293 cells without TurboID does not change with or
without addition of biotin in the cell culture media. We expect the same to be the case in vivo as
well. To confirm this, we performed an additional in vivo experiment in wild-type, Cx3cr1-
CreERT2, Camk2a-CreERT2 and neuron-TurboID mice and assessed the extend of biotinylation
signal via bulk brain immunoblot with either no biotin or 2 weeks of biotin water. We found that
the level of endogenous biotinylation in brain lysates from wild-type mice (without exogenous
biotin supplementation) and non-TurboID animals (with exogenous biotin supplementation) is the
same (please see figure below for the reviewer only), although we have not performed SPARO
studies on these ‘negative’ conditions. While it may also seem intuitive to have a neuron-TurboID
group without biotin, this is not an ideal control because (1) even without biotin supplementation,
the presence of TurboID will lead to biotinylation using biotin in regular chow, and (2) excessive
biotinylation by TurboID without supplementation, will lead to a relative biotin deficiency which will
be toxic to mice and create a significant confound.
We have also added our rationale for the 24-hour (in vitro) and two-week (in vivo) biotin
treatment duration to the methods section of the manuscript.
3. There is also probably one more set of experiments needed to understand the noise of
the method in general (see ‘Is the Methodology Sound’ section).
Response: In response to this concern, and to better quantify the level of noise in this system,
we performed a new set of experiments. Our goal was to understand what RNAs we would
“enrich” in non-TurboID samples, which could be defined as the background noise in the system.
Therefore, we performed differential enrichment analysis of the pulldown transcriptome between
the BV2 non-TurboID controls (n = 2 biological replicates, lanes 4 and 5 indicated by black arrows
in panel a below) and the BV2-TurboID (n = 3 biological replicates, lanes 10-12 indicated by green
arrow in panel a below) samples treated with LPS.
The “noise” that we found consisted primarily of many non-coding RNAs (e.g., Gdap10, Xist and
Malat1), pseudogenes (e.g., H2-K2 and Pisd-ps1) and splicing factors (e.g., Luc7l3 and Rsrp1)
enriched in the BV2 non-TurboID LPS controls. We predict that these transcripts are enriched in
the BV2 non-TurboID controls simply because they are generally highly abundant in mammalian
cells7–9.
We also found that Acaca is a highly abundant transcript in the BV2 non-TurboID controls. Acaca
is an endogenously biotinylated protein10,11 that is a rate-limiting enzyme in fatty acid synthesis
(converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA)12. We hypothesize that the Acaca protein can regulate its
own regulation via interaction with Acaca transcript. Indeed, one paper in 201913 provided
evidence for interaction between a bacterial carboxypeptidase (equivalent to mammalian Acaca)
and its mRNA, provide a ‘dimmer’ type regulatory mechanism for a rate-limiting metabolic enzyme
to regulate mRNA to protein translation via direct protein-mRNA interaction.
It is also possible that these RNA species interact with endogenously biotinylated proteins10,11
allowing them to be captured from non-TurboID RNA pulldowns. It is also important to note here,
that only LPS-treated BV2 non-TurboID-derived RNA pulldowns yielded cDNA libraries for RNA-
seq while those from non-LPS BV2 non-TurboID cells did not. There may be several possible
explanations for why the noise RNA pulldowns may change with LPS treatment, some due to
technical reasons and some potentially biological reasons. While we cannot resolve these
possibilities in this study, users of SPARO must plan to use several different non-TurboID
negative control pulldowns to account for these variabilities in experiments. These data have been
added to Supplementary Fig. 2 and provided below.
4. Figure S7d: TurboID and RiboTag have substantial differences (thousands of DEGs in
Figure S10) that are rather underplayed here. I would recommend a couple of analyses digging
into these differences more. Maybe something similar to what they do in Figure S10?
Response: Thank you to the reviewer for their insightful recommendation. We agree that
additional analyses like Supplementary Fig. 10 is helpful to investigate differences between the
astrocyte-TurboID and astrocyte-RiboTag pulldown transcriptomes.
For this new analysis, we investigated the average transcript length, percent GC content, and
number of exons using bioMart/ENSEMBL of the highly enriched DEGs in the astrocyte-TurboID
versus astrocyte-RiboTag differential gene expression analysis from Supplementary Fig. 9d (via
p ≤ 0.05, ≥ 1-log -fold change). We found that all three RNA characteristics are significantly
2
different between the SPARO TurboID and RiboTag-enriched astrocytic transcriptomes. Mean
transcript length (****p < 0.0001, Mann Whitney test), and exon number (*p = 0.029, Mann-
Whitney test) were higher in the TurboID pulldowns while percent GC content (**p = 0.002, Mann
Whitney test) was higher in the RiboTag pulldowns. These differences may reflect the broader
nature of TurboID labeling, which captures many RNA-binding proteins not limited to those
associated with active translation.
We also found a significant difference in the average percent GC content between the astrocyte-
TurboID and astrocyte-RiboTag pulldowns. We predict that this may be indirectly related to
transcript length. The average percent GC content may also be related to the classes, or functions
of transcripts captured by each method. There is also the possibility that because the RiboTag
approach is primarily biased towards ribosome-associated, actively translated mRNAs, that these
transcripts are more enriched in housekeeping transcripts with a higher GC content. In contrast,
TurboID labeling may recover a broader pool of RNA-interacting proteins, including those
associated with longer, less GC-rich transcripts at earlier stages of RNA processing. We have
now included this new analysis in Supplementary Fig. 9g and below for the reviewer.
It is possible that TurboID biotinylates RNA-interacting proteins at multiple stages of the mRNA
life cycle, including during nuclear processing events such as splicing, consistent with the
expectation that pre-spliced transcripts are generally longer and contain more exons than
ribosome-associated, spliced mRNAs.
We predict that these differences may be associated with the nature of TurboID biotinylating many
proteins that interact with RNA that are not only being actively translated. To further investigate
this, we also performed MS on proteins enriched by the RiboTag pulldown and contrasted these
proteomes with SPARO pulldown proteomes, expecting to find differences in how each approach
can differentially enrich ribosomal and RNA-binding proteins, thereby explaining differences in the
RiboTag translatome and SPARO transcriptomes (see new Fig. 3f and g provided below and
Reviewer 2, Comment 27 response). As predicted, RiboTag pulldown captures a smaller cadre
of RNA-binding and larger proportion of ribosomal (translational) proteins, while SPARO captures
many more RNA-binding proteins while also capturing many ribosomal proteins, albeit with some
differences across methods.
It may be possible that TurboID is capable of biotinylating RNA-interacting proteins at different
stages of the mRNA life cycle (e.g., TurboID biotinylates an RNA-binding protein that translocate
to the nucleus to assist with mRNA processing such as splicing). It is likely that pre-spliced
transcripts (assessable by biotinylated RNA-binding proteins) are generally longer than post-
spliced transcripts (i.e., transcripts associated with ribosomes for translation).
Taken together, our new analyses provide several probable reasons for observed differences
between SPARO and RiboTag transcriptomes, despite their strong correlations. We certainly see
examining these differences as a future direction of the SPARO approach.
We have now included this analysis in Fig 3f and g and Supplementary Fig. 9g as well as
in the results and discussion sections.
5. The authors spend some time on page 8 speculating why the transcriptome and proteome
are sometimes discordant. One additional source of such discordance could simply be cellular
compartment: it seems like even in vivo the TURBO-ID is restricted to the cytoplasm? Yet the
transcripts that code for all proteins in the cell (nuclear, mitochondria, etc), are largely
translated in the cytoplasm. So some of the discordance could simply reflect that the mature translated
protein ends up somewhere in the cell where it cannot be readily tagged. Likewise, any excreted
proteins might be lost to TurboID labeling (including potentially Lcn2, which they highlight in their
discussion). When the come back discussing discordance on page 10, they do bring up this
possibility that it is driven by cellular compartments in part. However, they may wish to revise
these sections, as the different cellular compartments is probably the simplest explanation and
should be raised earlier.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this issue. For both the in vitro and in vivo
SPARO experiments, the TurboID construct contains a nuclear export sequence. Therefore,
TurboID is localized to the cytosol of the cell. We have added immunocytochemistry images of
the BV2 non-TurboID control and BV2-TurboID microglial cells in culture to emphasize that the
presence of TurboID via V5 and biotinylation signal is primarily in the cytosol. Please see ICC
images added to Supplementary Fig. 1a and below. Moreover, at the transcriptomic-level
comparing the BV2-TurboID pulldowns versus global samples (+/- LPS treatment), we find that
the majority of DEGs upregulated in the global group are mitochondrial-encoded transcripts (e.g.,
COX1, CYTB and ND1). This provides additional evidence that the TurboID enzyme is biased
away from the mitochondrial compartment. Please see Supplementary Fig. 4a and b.
We have now revised this section and brought it up earlier as suggested to better highlight
the cytosolic localization of TurboID being a contributing factor to discordance between
the transcriptome and proteome.
In addition, to address the next point in Comment 6, we performed a new SPARO experiment in
HEK293 cells comparing the transcriptomes and proteomes of TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES
pulldowns. This new experiment is now included in the manuscript as Supplementary Figs. 15-
19).
6. The difficulty in interpreting RNA/Protein comparisons is the part of the paper I find the
most challenging and that would make me hesitant to bring the approach into my own lab. Is there
anything that could be done informatically to address this? For example, if they limit the analysis
comparing RNA to Protein to the proteins that are in the cytoplasm (potentially by GO),
does the correlation improve between RNA and Protein? Does the ability to use things like protein half lives
(or perhaps codon usage) to predict Protein/RNA discordance improve? And can they start to look
at cell differences in RNA/Protein discordance in a more insightful way if limiting their analysis to
proteins that have a better chance of being tagged (i.e., the cytoplasmic ones)? On the whole,
this comparisons seems to be one of the motivating aspects of the paper, so it would be
nice to have some recommendations on how to approach these questions with the current technique. (I
appreciate that the authors also discuss future method changes like removing the NES that might
address this experimentally).
Response: We certainly take this concern to heart, and it was shared by other reviewers as well.
Therefore, to better experimentally address the limitations of the cytosolic TurboID (TurboID-NES),
we conducted a new in vitro SPARO experiment in HEK293 cells with a TurboID construct
that lacks the NES.
We found that the noNES versus NES pulldown transcriptomes are highly similar (92% overlap
in transcripts detected and mRNA abundances highly correlated r = 0.99, Supplementary Fig
15e and fbelow). We found a similar trend with the pulldown proteomes (85% overlap in peptides
detected and protein abundances highly correlated r = 0.93, Supplementary Fig 15e and g
below). Moreover, when we assessed the correlation between the paired pulldown
transcriptomes and proteomes, the correlation is similar between the TurboID-noNES and NES
SPARO approaches (r = 0.31 (NES) and 0.35 (noNES), Supplementary Fig 15l and m below).
Together, these findings suggest that the noNES and NES TurboID enzymes in vitro yield similar
proteomic and even more similar transcriptomic profiles and that removing the NES to restrict
TurboID to the cytoplasm does not greatly increase the correlation between mRNA-protein
abundances. Moreover, these findings suggest that the mRNA-protein correlation being modest
is likely not simply explained away by the compartment restriction of TurboID.
We have also made a new Rosa26-TurboID mouse line without the NES and the line is currently
being validated. We fully intend on applying the SPARO approach using this new mouse, but we
are at least 2 years away from a definitive experiment to confirm that the in vitro noNES versus
NES findings translate in vivo.
We have adjusted the manuscript by adding the new HEK293 TurboID-NES versus noNES
SPARO study to Supplementary Fig. 15 and below for the reviewer.
Comment 6 response continued:
To address the reviewer’s recommendation to limit the correlation analysis to cytosolic proteins,
we also performed this analysis by filtering the proteins based on the bioMart/ENSEMBL GO term
ID for cytosol "GO:0005829" and provided the data for the reviewer below. After filtering for
cytosolic proteins (n = 626 - 742), we found that the correlation between the abundance of mRNAs
and proteins remains modest (r = 0.28 – 0.36), similar to the unfiltered correlation plots in
Supplementary Fig. 11 (r = 0.24 - 0.27).
We have provided the correlation plots below for the reviewer and briefly mentioned this
finding in the discussion section of the manuscript.
7. Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
They need to better account for sex in their work (and in future studies, may want to balance for

reactive intermediate, biotin-AMP that can be quickly added to lysine residues of proteins that are
close-by15,16.
However, within a cell, there is not enough endogenous biotin to support sufficient labeling of
cellular proteins leading to poor signal in streptavidin pulldowns1. Additionally, because the
TurboID enzyme is efficient in using free biotin to tag proteins, this creates a competition for a
cell’s normal machinery that critically needs biotin (e.g., carboxylase enzymes for different
metabolic pathways)10. Therefore, exogenous biotin supplementation is standard in TurboID
proximity labeling protocols.

our original in vivo TurboID paper4 showing that whole cell biotinylation levels in HEK293 cells
without TurboID does not change with or without addition of biotin in the cell culture media. We
expect the same to be the case in vivo as well. To confirm this, we performed an additional in vivo
experiment in wild-type, Cx3cr1-CreERT2 (no TurboID), Camk2a-CreERT2 (no TurboID) and
neuron (Camk2a)-TurboID mice and assessed the extend of biotinylation signal via bulk brain
immunoblot with either no biotin or 2 weeks of biotin water. We found that the level of endogenous
biotinylation in brain lysates from wild-type mice (without exogenous biotin supplementation) and
non-TurboID animals (with exogenous biotin supplementation) is the same (please see figure
below for the reviewer only), although we have not performed SPARO studies on these
‘negative’ conditions. While it may also seem intuitive to have a neuron-TurboID group without
biotin, this is not an ideal control because (1) even without biotin supplementation, the presence
of TurboID will lead to biotinylation using biotin in regular chow, and (2) excessive biotinylation by
TurboID without supplementation, will lead to a relative biotin deficiency which will be toxic to mice
and create a significant confound.

Together, we believe these findings suggest that the discordant phenotypes seen in the

Regarding validation of discordant markers, we have thought deeply about this validation query
but there are many challenges to addressing this is a rigorous manner. To validate a
mRNA>protein hit, we need a highly precise and sensitive manner to measure both the mRNA
and protein using an approach that is not MS. Antibody-based measures of protein (in
immunofluorescence microscopy) are not linear with absolute protein abundances and as the
reviewer knows, suffer from many failures due to poorly validated proteins. For mRNA, the
approach of choice likely includes RNA-scope or other in situ hybridization approaches. While this
may be measuring the mRNA level, the protein measurement will be lacking, making it very
challenging to truly validate a mRNA>protein or for that matter, a protein>mRNA target as well.

many of the used antibodies show signal, which is not very convincing, and are limited to few
antibody vendors. Therefore, we do not feel confident is using these sources for validation studies.
While we used MS for all of our studies, we also point out that there is independent validation of
these across datasets which include different cell types. Using bulk tissues, neuron-specific and
astrocyte-specific -omes, we arrived at similar types of mRNA-protein pairs in concordant and
discordant groups, suggesting that are indeed capturing biological phenomena rather than
findings due to random chance.

again providing an additional layer of validation. We therefore humbly suggest that our findings
are more about types of mRNA-protein pairs that tend to be concordant or discordant, rather than
about identifying specific pairs for validation. We have therefore also decreased the emphasis on
specific genes/proteins in this analysis, but rather focused on shared ontologies.
